How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Recent debates about psychology's credibility have renewed attention to validity threats. We argue that pilot studies can function as methodological due diligence by improving early decisions about design, measurement, manipulation, sampling, and analysis prior to a main study. We examine four types of validity: construct, internal, external, and statistical-conclusion validity. Across these domains, we list ways in which piloting can help researchers assess whether materials and procedures function as intended, identify potential validity threats, and provide key design parameters for planning and model choice. However, we also caution that piloting can harm validity when treated as a consequence-free space in which design or analytic choices are made without disclosing the pilot evidence behind them, or when small, noisy pilots are used to justify overconfident inferences. We therefore argue that when pilots are used to justify substantive design or analytic choices, they should be treated as part of the evidential record and reported transparently. Greater transparency would enable readers to evaluate how pilot evidence shaped the final design of a study and, consequently, better assess the validity of its findings.

[div-01]

"Like most social-psychological experiments, the experiments reported here required extensive pilot testing. As all research psychologists know, many procedures are tried and discarded during this process. This raises the question of how much of this pilot exploration should be reported to avoid the file-drawer problem, the selective suppression of negative or null results." -Daryl J. Bem (2011, p. 421), Feeling the Future: Experimental Evidence for

Anomalous Retroactive Influences on Cognition and Affect

Psychology has spent over a decade grappling with a "crisis of confidence" (Lakens, 2025; Nosek et al., 2022; Pashler & Wagenmakers, 2012), with the early focal point of Bem's (2011) Journal of Personality and Social Psychology report on apparent precognition effects. Scrutiny of Bem's findings (Wagenmakers et al., 2011), alongside widespread replicability issues (Open Science Collaboration, 2015), prompted broad reconsideration of the individual practices researchers use to generate findings and how the field evaluates their credibility after publication. In addition to motivating measures that increase transparency (e.g., preregistration, Registered Reports, open data, open materials), these credibility concerns have also renewed attention to research validity (e.g., see Vazire et al., 2022). In this article, we argue that piloting offers a practical, and often overlooked, way to address validity concerns, provided it is reported transparently.

Concerns about validity have become a topic of particular interest in social and personality psychology. Hussey and Hughes (2020), for example, found that 88% of 26 commonly used scales in these fields appeared adequate when assessed using internal consistency alone, yet only 4% met their criterion for good structural validity. More recently, Lawson et al. (2026) found that basic measurement information needed to evaluate construct validity is inconsistently reported in social and personality psychology articles. They also found that nearly half of the measures they examined were created ad hoc, leaving no prior validity evidence for authors or readers to draw on. Recent work converges on the fact that researchers need not only ways to identify potential validity threats, but also practical ways to determine whether those threats are present in their own planned studies early enough to make adjustments (Kerschbaumer et al., 2025; Schiavone et al., 2023).

Part of the difficulty of validity assessment is that validity is not a single, unified concern. Each of the four major forms of validity outlined by Shadish et al. (2002)-construct, internal, external, and statistical-conclusion-addresses a different aspect of the research process: from the accuracy of measurement and the fidelity of manipulations, to the soundness of causal inference and the generalizability of findings (Chester, 2018 (Chester, , 2020;; Chester & Lasko, 2021; Flake & Fried, 2020; Nosek & Errington, 2020; Rohrer, 2018; Yarkoni, 2022). Addressing all of these aspects of the research process can be challenging, especially when researchers are increasingly expected to plan, justify, and communicate a wide range of design and analysis decisions before the consequences of those choices are known (or knowable).

For example, preregistration and Registered Reports require researchers to specify design and analysis decisions before observing the main-study data to constrain data-contingent flexibility (Lakens et al., 2024; van den Akker et al., 2024). While these practices can improve transparency and allow for prospective methodological scrutiny, they do not by themselves ensure that the decisions specified are well-suited to the study. Researchers must still decide which measures, procedures, exclusion rules, models, and other specifications to use before they necessarily know how those choices will function in practice.

Unsurprisingly, researchers often find such detailed study planning difficult in practice (see Hahn et al., 2025; Lakens, 2024; Nosek et al., 2019; Sarafoglou et al., 2022), and plans can vary between being too vague (i.e., leaving many analytic paths open) and overly rigid (i.e., locking in arbitrary decisions ill-suited to unexpected problems). We propose that one way to alleviate these difficulties and address validity challenges is to transparently gather information on validity-relevant aspects of the study before the main data collection: in other words, to pilot.

Pilotingfoot_0 broadly describes the iterative process of conducting preparatory investigations before investing in the full-scale or "main" study (In, 2017). Although often construed as merely procedural (Arain et al., 2010; National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, n.d.; Thabane et al., 2010), piloting decisions are validity-relevant: operationalizing an idea into a working methodology ultimately involves generating empirical evidence that justifies methodological and analytical choices. For example, pilots can be used to inform decisions that must be finalized before data collection begins (e.g., materials, instructions, task structure) or guide decisions that must be specified in advance but only take effect after data collection (e.g., exclusion criteria, model selection, outlier handling).

We advance the perspective that when implemented carefully, piloting can improve design decisions, and when reported transparently, it can also help readers and reviewers evaluate the basis for those decisions. In the following subsections, drawing on Shadish et al.'s (2002) validity framework, we illustrate representative threats for each validity type and how pilots can address them (the "Promises"). We then discuss how piloting can itself undermine validity when basic principles of inference are not followed (the "Pitfalls"). Figure 1 summarizes these uses across the four validities, and Figure 2 the corresponding pitfalls. In the Discussion, we outline conceptual and practical ways to navigate these promises and pitfalls of piloting and argue that, no matter the piloting approach committed to, doing so transparently is the precondition for addressing validity concerns.

Promises of Piloting

In the following subsections, we list ways in which piloting can provide validity-relevant information. These use-cases are not intended as an exhaustive checklist: which are most useful will depend on the study's intended claims and the validity-relevant uncertainties researchers have about their planned design. Additionally, because validity threats can overlap, a single pilot may address several concerns simultaneously.

Piloting for Construct Validity

Construct validity refers to whether a study's operationalizations provide a defensible link between abstract theory and participants' experiences and responses (Cronbach & Meehl, 1955; Flake & Fried, 2020). Many threats arise from disconnects between theory and practice. For example, researchers may use "construct labels" that are clearer to experts than to participants, rely on measures that behave differently than anticipated, or employ manipulations that shape responses through demand cues rather than through the intended psychological process. Piloting can help determine whether proposed measures and procedures function as the theory assumes in several ways.

First, qualitative and mixed-methods piloting, such as think-aloud protocols (e.g., Ericsson & Crutcher, 1991; Foddy, 1993; Wolcott & Lobczowski, 2021) or open-ended feedback, can assess whether participants interpret construct labels, interview questions, item content, and instructions as intended (e.g., Beatty & Willis, 2007; Irwin et al., 2009; Padilla & Benítez, 2014). For example, cognitive interviews can help researchers check whether participants understand questionnaire content (e.g., Oľhová et al., 2023), open-ended questions can reveal how participants interpret items (e.g., Schönbrodt et al., 2022), and pilot administration of new instruments or materials can identify where instructions or explanations need refinement (e.g., Eisele et al., 2025; Neff et al., 2025).

Second, pilots allow for an initial evaluation of measurement quality. Researchers can estimate internal consistency and test-retest reliability, examine item distributions, including floor and ceiling effects, inspect factor structure, and detect response patterns indicative of inattentive responding or demand characteristics (Coles et al., 2025; Corneille & Lush, 2023; Johanson & Brooks, 2010). For example, test-retest reliability of an instrument can be estimated by administering the planned measure twice in a pilot sample (e.g., Hundley et al., 2000), and pilot data can inform adjustments to task parameters when the original task produces floor or ceiling effects (e.g., Loenneker et al., 2024; McDougal et al., 2024).

Third, pilots can validate manipulations. By measuring the intended construct alongside plausible alternatives, researchers can check a manipulation's discriminant validity (i.e., whether it primarily affects the target construct rather than related but unintended constructs, such as arousal instead of anger; e.g., Hauser et al., 2018) and identify unintended side effects (Chester & Lasko, 2021; Fabrigar et al., 2020; Schiavone et al., 2023). For example, preliminary testing can identify and reject manipulations that participants find too transparent or that fail to produce the intended effect (e.g., Baumeister et al., 1998; Le et al., 2026; Zygar-Hoffmann et al., 2022), and refine design parameters and hypotheses before a confirmatory main study (e.g., Brohmer et al., 2024; Hajdu et al., 2022).

Fourth, pilots can also calibrate stimulus sets and novel paradigms to confirm they have the intended properties. For example, pilot data can be used to match stimulus subsets on multiple relevant dimensions (Nagel et al., 2024), to validate stimuli to ensure they measure the intended construct and avoid confounds (Neff, 2024), and to validate a novel paradigm before deployment in a confirmatory study (Schäfer et al., 2022).

Finally, pilots can test whether translations preserve the intended constructs across languages. They can also help researchers assess whether materials are culturally appropriate for the target population (Baldassarri & Abascal, 2017; A. R. Kenny, 2021; Pit et al., 2024).

Piloting for Internal Validity

Internal validity refers to whether observed effects can be attributed to the intended causal variable rather than to alternative explanations, such as confounding factors, differential attrition, or implementation differences (Campbell & Stanley, 1963; D. A. Kenny, 2019). Threats to causal interpretation arise when participants are not comparable between conditions, procedures are inconsistently implemented, blinding fails, or other unintended differences exist between conditions. In observational designs, threats include unmeasured confounding, selection bias, and order effects (Rohrer, 2018). Piloting can help assess and address these threats through several distinct approaches.

First, piloting can screen for unintended confounds in stimuli, materials, and procedures. By testing stimulus matching, procedural details, and implementation, researchers can identify and eliminate sources of systematic variation between conditions before the main study begins. For example, pilots can allow researchers to compare alternative implementations of a procedure to avoid unintended effects on the dependent variable (e.g., David et al., 2021; Neff et al., 2025), refine procedural details such as trial structure, ordering, or outlier-treatment procedures (Greenwald et al., 1998), and validate stimulus sets and ensure that their subsets are matched on relevant dimensions (Nagel et al., 2024; Neff, 2024).

Second, piloting can verify the randomization by running the planned assignment process and examining whether resulting groups are comparable on key background variables. Researchers can then adjust recruitment strategies, introduce balancing procedures, or pre-plan statistical adjustments if imbalances emerge.

Third, piloting can probe participant blinding and sensitivity to demand or experimenter effects by asking participants (and researchers when double-blinding is required) what they think the study is about and whether they can guess their condition (Slack & Draugalis, 2001).

Fourth, pilots can evaluate counterbalancing schemes and task length. This, in turn, can help identify and reduce fatigue or order effects in the design.

Finally, pilots can map attrition dynamics by tracking dropout rates and reasons across conditions and identifying when procedures may need revision (e.g., McDougal et al., 2024).

Piloting for External Validity

External validity refers to the extent to which findings generalize beyond the specific sample, stimuli (including treatments and manipulations), measurements, and settings (including time points) studied (Campbell, 1957; D. A. Kenny, 2019). Common threats include vague generalization targets, narrow or poorly described samples, and dependence on specific sample characteristics. Pilots can help researchers clarify the likely scope of their conclusions across several dimensions of generalization.

First, piloting can inform sampling and recruitment decisions. Researchers can recruit small pilot samples from different sources or channels and compare them on demographics, key covariates, and outcome distributions, refining eligibility criteria or sampling strategies on this basis (e.g., Dyrvig et al., 2014; Slack & Draugalis, 2001). For example, pilots can test whether a planned recruitment approach reaches a specific intended population, such as a clinical group (Loenneker et al., 2024) or couples in romantic relationships (Le et al., 2026; Zygar-Hoffmann et al., 2022).

Second, stimulus sets can be piloted more broadly to estimate between-stimulus variance and calibrate difficulty before selecting a subset for the main study. By piloting a larger pool than will be used in the main study, researchers can characterize how responses vary across stimuli and exclude items that fall below a quality threshold (e.g., ambiguous items, items at floor or ceiling, or items with low reliabilityfoot_1 ), provided that exclusion does not depend on the size of the effect an item produces. Because effects that depend strongly on particular stimuli may not generalize to the broader stimulus population, the estimated between-stimulus variance can also inform the likely scope of generalization and how stimulus variation should be modeled in the main analysis. For example, researchers can pilot a large set of candidate items (faces, words, scenarios) and select a balanced subset that represents the relevant range of stimuli for the main study.

Third, pilots can assess procedural robustness across settings, devices, and task instantiations. Running the same task online and in the lab, on mobile and desktop, at different times, or across task versions can reveal systematic differences that may warrant standardizing procedures. For example, pilots can use such comparisons to identify procedural variants that may affect generalization (e.g., David et al., 2021; Elsherif et al., 2022) and to determine when procedures need revision for use with particular populations (McDougal et al., 2024).

Finally, piloting can test cultural and contextual fit by checking whether translations and examples are interpretable across subgroups (Baldassarri & Abascal, 2017; A. R. Kenny, 2021). For example, pilots can validate materials prior to cross-cultural studies (Pit et al., 2024) and help adapt instruments for populations or contexts the original was not designed for (Oľhová et al., 2023).

Piloting for Statistical-Conclusion Validity

Statistical-conclusion validity refers to the appropriateness of statistical analyses and inferences given the study's design, underlying assumptions, and data quality (Cook & Campbell, 1979; D. A. Kenny, 2019; Shadish et al., 2002). Common threats include weakly justified sample sizes, unclear stopping or exclusion rules, mismatches between hypotheses and statistical models, overly rigid preanalysis plans based on assumptions that do not match the observed data, and opaque reporting. Piloting can provide design parameters and modeling insights at multiple stages of the analytic trajectory that are difficult to obtain before data collection.

First, pilots can estimate auxiliary parameters that are needed for design planning but are usually unknown in advance. Pilot data can help estimate outcome variance (Teare et al., 2014), intraclass correlations (Snijders & Bosker, 2012), baseline-outcome correlations (Borm et al., 2007), rates of missing data (Heo, 2014), and typical numbers of valid trials per participant (Miller, 2024). These estimates can support more realistic sample-size justifications and help determine cluster sizes and expected data loss (Bolger & Laurenceau, 2013). For example, pilots have been used to estimate test-retest reliability of a planned measure (Hundley et al., 2000), and to refine design parameters in coordinated pre-studies before a multi-lab confirmatory test (Brohmer et al., 2024).

Second, pilot analyses can help identify appropriate model families before committing to the main analysis. Using pilot data, researchers can examine features such as overdispersion, zero inflation, residual skew, floor or ceiling effects, or the stability of proposed random-effects structures (De Boeck & Jeon, 2018; Dyrvig et al., 2014), and then preregister an appropriate model for the focal test. If the pilot's sample size is large enough, it can help detect the features that matter for the modeling decision. For example, pilots have been used to evaluate a reliability model for nested experiencesampling data (Schönbrodt et al., 2022) and to validate a novel paradigm before deploying it in a confirmatory test (Schäfer et al., 2022). This use pays off particularly when a modeling choice cannot be specified in advance. When it can, preregistering a decision rule may be preferable to relying on a pilot. When a pilot does inform the choice, however, what matters is the basis for it: selecting a model because the pilot data violate the assumptions of the alternatives is a modeling decision, whereas selecting whichever model produces the largest focal effect turns the pilot into a hidden model-selection stage.

Third, pilots can inform data-handling rules by revealing realistic response time ranges and plausible thresholds for excluding trials or participants (Fabrigar et al., 2020; Thomas & Clifford, 2017). For example, pilots can be used to refine outlier-treatment procedures and exclusion thresholds before the main analysis (Greenwald et al., 1998).

Finally, pilot experience can clarify which outcomes and contrasts are substantively relevant, helping anticipate multiplicity and distinguish confirmatory from exploratory analyses (Ditroilo et al., 2025; Li et al., 2017). Examining pilot data can identify which contrasts will be informative to test in the main study and which would yield ambiguous results. Pre-specifying confirmatory tests on this basis reduces the number of comparisons that need correction and makes the boundary between confirmatory and exploratory analyses explicit in the eventual report.

Pitfalls of Piloting Practices

Parameter Estimation from Low-Precision Pilots

Many pitfalls arise when pilots are treated as exempt from basic statistical constraints. Pilot studies may, and perhaps often will, be smaller than main studies because their aims are narrower and more diagnostic. However, labeling a study "a pilot" does not exempt it from the usual constraints of scientific inference. Limited sample size, selective recruitment, and contextual specificity still shape what can be learned from a pilot. Accordingly, a "pilot sample" should not be treated as synonymous with a "small convenience sample," and there is no principle by which a study stops being a pilot once its sample becomes large.

Nevertheless, pilots are commonly used in practice to estimate quantities that inform main-study decisions, such as effect sizes, variances, intraclass correlations, reliabilities, and attrition rates, although not all of these uses are equally well justified. When pilots are small, these estimates are noisy, and decisions made on the basis of noisy estimates can be unstable (Lewis et al., 2021). Sampling error alone can produce apparent effects in a pilot that will not replicate, or obscure effects that do exist. These problems take different forms across the four validities. For construct validity, small samples give imprecise estimates of reliability (Bonett, 2002; Charter, 2003; Johanson & Brooks, 2010) or factor structure (MacCallum et al., 1999), leading to false reassurance or unjustified item pruning (Clark & Watson, 1995). For internal validity, small-sample pilots may lack the power to detect modest but important imbalances or demand effects, and the absence of detected problems does not imply their absence in the main study (Cooper et al., 2018). For external validity, small or convenience samples may give an incomplete picture of which populations are reachable or how heterogeneous responses will be. For statistical-conclusion validity, treating small-sample effect-size estimates as accurate inputs for power analyses or for specifying the smallest effect size of interest is particularly risky (Lakens et al., 2018). For example, simulations show that basing main-study designs on small-sample pilot effect sizes tends to produce underpowered studies (Albers & Lakens, 2018; Lakens, 2022).

The bias is not symmetric. Although pilot estimates are noisy in both directions, they become systematically inflated when researchers act on "promising" pilot outcomes, such as statistical significance or feasibility. Selecting from a truncated subset of the sampling distribution can inflate the effect size used in subsequent power analyses (Albers & Lakens, 2018). The same logic extends beyond power analysis. If a small-sample pilot suggests that participants completing the study on mobile devices produce noisier data than those using desktop devices, for example, it may be tempting to exclude them from the main study. Yet whether this is warranted depends on the magnitude and uncertainty of the observed difference, the theoretical justifications for and implications of such an exclusion, and the recruitment constraints of the pilot. Treating such differences as decisive risks overfitting the design to pilot idiosyncrasies.

However, none of this is to say that pilots are inherently imprecise or that researchers must overhaul their approach or exhaust their resources to make pilots worthwhile. Rather, because pilots commonly use small samples, it is important to recognize the constraints this entails. The sampling variability of pilot estimates needs to be taken into account when deciding how the pilot will inform choices. Where precision matters for a specific aim (e.g., estimating an auxiliary parameter used in sample-size planning), the pilot should be designed accordingly (see Johanson & Brooks, 2010, for pilot-sample recommendations in scale development). Otherwise, small-sample estimates should be considered as rough guides rather than decisive inputs and calibrated against previous studies or field norms. We return to this in the Discussion ("Calibrating Confidence in Pilot-Informed Decisions").

Selection from Multiple Pilot Variants Without Disclosure

A second pitfall arises when pilots are used to select among multiple variants of a study element (e.g., stimuli, measurements, recruitment channels, or analytic specifications) and the selection process is not disclosed. When the variant retained for the main study is chosen on the basis of which produced the most favorable result, the pilot becomes a hidden exploratory stage that can bias the main study's confirmatory test.

This pattern manifests across the four validities. For construct validity, measures or manipulations can be "over-tuned" through repeated piloting to produce "clean" effects, narrowing the construct, distorting its meaning, or introducing demand effects by making the design too obvious to the participant. For internal validity, running many design variants during piloting and selecting the version that produces the largest effect, without disclosing this search, shifts threats from the main study to the pilot stage rather than resolving them. For external validity, stimulus piloting can become "stimulus hacking" (Experimental Philosophy, 2025; Jaeger, 2023) when researchers test a large pool of stimuli and retain only those producing large effects without reporting the selection process, so that the reported effect may hold for the selected items without generalizing to the broader stimulus population. For statistical-conclusion validity, using pilots to try many analytic models or transformations and then selecting the one that yields the most favorable results makes the pilot a hidden model-selection stage. This resembles p-hacking in that observed data are used to select among analytic specifications, but the consequences differ. Selecting on the main-study data inflates the false-positive rate of the reported test, whereas selecting on an independent pilot leaves that rate at its nominal level and costs severity instead. A test is severe when it is likely to yield supporting results if the substantive claim is true but unlikely to yield them through mechanisms unrelated to the theory (Claesen et al., 2022). A specification retained for having produced a favorable result may track features of the pilot that are real and reproducible yet unrelated to the theory, so the main study can replicate an effect narrower than the claim it is presented as supporting.

Such practices have been documented across psychology, including in simulation work on pilotdropping (i.e., running an initial pilot, inspecting its p-value, and proceeding only when results look promising) versus pilot-hacking (i.e., tuning an analytic specification on the pilot data until a small p-value emerges, then continuing data collection and analyzing the combined data with that specification as a single dataset; see Simonsohn et al., 2018) and in critiques of how stimulus selection shapes published findings (Yarkoni, 2022). The two are not equivalent: pilot-dropping leaves the main study's error rate intact, whereas pilot-hacking merges the samples and therefore inflates it. The common feature is that the search process is hidden, so that the published main study appears to test a hypothesis that has in fact been adjusted to fit the pilot data, eroding the severity of any subsequent test (Claesen et al., 2022; Lakens, 2019; Rubin, 2025).

Mismatch and Contamination Between Pilot and Main Study

A third pitfall arises at the interface between the pilot and the main study, when the two are not aligned in conditions or analyses. For internal validity, if the main study departs from the pilot in its recruitment sources, instructions, experimenters, or other implementation details, the assurances obtained from piloting may no longer hold (see also Johanson & Brooks, 2010). Pilot-based checks of randomization, blinding, or balance were established under specific conditions that the main study must replicate for those checks to remain informative.

For statistical-conclusion validity, similar problems arise when pilot data are included in the main analysis without proper adjustments, or when the boundary between pilot and main samples is unclear (In, 2017). In such cases, the same data both motivate and test the confirmatory claim, with consequences for the probability of a false positive (for a detailed examination of this issue, see Schott et al., 2019). The role of any pilot data should therefore be specified in advance, including whether they will be combined with main data and under what adjustments, and reported transparently so that readers can evaluate the inferential basis of the main study's test.

Discussion

Recent methodological and metascientific work has renewed attention to validity threats in study design and reporting (Kerschbaumer et al., 2025; Schiavone et al., 2023), particularly in social and personality psychology (e.g., Hussey & Hughes, 2020; Lawson et al., 2026). We have argued that piloting can provide early, validity-relevant information before main data collection. Yet the same flexibility that makes piloting useful also creates risks, making it reasonable to question how much value piloting adds or whether it is worth the effort.

When pilot studies are used to justify decisions about measures, designs, or analyses, they function as scientific evidence, and the same principles of validity and inference that apply to the main study apply to piloting as well. In this sense, the pitfalls are not unique to piloting. They are inherent to research design more broadly, but become especially visible in piloting because of the ways these studies are typically conducted and because they are, at best, rarely reported. The discussion that follows develops conceptual and practical implications of this position.

Defining "Piloting"

Piloting practices vary widely across studies and research areas, including the terms used and understandings of what counts as a pilot. This variation likely contributes to vagueness about what piloting is and what it can achieve. One might respond by advocating stricter boundaries, but this is not our approach. Instead, the functional definition we use in this paper holds that main studies adjudicate focal claims, while pilots inform and refine decisions about how to conduct main studies.

We take the defining feature of a pilot to be its relationship to a subsequent main study, not its form. Accordingly, we draw the boundary by what the study investigates rather than how it is conducted. Under this view, pilots may serve as proofs of concept, sanity checks, feasibility studies, norming studies, manipulation or instrument checks, or combinations of these. This also distinguishes a pilot from an exploratory study of the same focal topic. An exploratory study may be open-ended in its hypotheses yet still investigate the focal relationship, whereas a pilot investigates methodological features rather than the focal relationship itself. 3A further implication is that resources do not determine whether a study is a pilot. Treating typical pilot characteristics, such as being small-sampled or cheap, as defining features can obscure its purpose and create poor incentives. For example, because pilot studies are frequently undervalued relative to main studies, researchers may feel pressure to reframe well-resourced pilots as main studies or avoid reporting pilot work altogether. But a well-resourced pilot is not a demoted main study, and a small pilot is not an inadequate study; they occupy different epistemic positions defined by what they are designed to inform.

Alternatively, one might argue for a narrower definition, such as limiting pilots to testing methodological feasibility while leaving the validation of manipulation effects to the main study (Kistin & Silverstein, 2015). However, the informational goals of piloting vary widely, and there is no clear boundary between its different uses. Trying to see if participants behave as the researchers intended, for instance, can be conceived as both a test of feasibility and a test of the method's effect; under the functional definition, that work can be classified as a pilot or as a separate main study, depending on what is being adjudicated. Enforcing a narrower definition would require stipulating specific permitted use-cases. Formalizing such a strict definition could therefore rule out widely used practices or force researchers to artificially separate inherently linked components that are not naturally separable.

Regardless of definitional stance, the pitfalls we document do not actually require a strict definition to be addressed. Problems associated with noisy small-sample estimates, undisclosed selection, and data contamination are not unique to piloting; they simply arise frequently at the boundaries between preparatory, exploratory, and confirmatory work. Since work at this boundary is not commonly reported, addressing these issues is less about what an activity is called than whether it is disclosed. Building on Handley-Miner et al. (2025), we therefore propose that whenever a pilot is used to motivate choices in a main study, it should be treated as part of the evidential record and reported transparently.

Calibrating Confidence in Pilot-Informed Decisions

Many of the pitfalls we describe arise from small or low-precision pilots. As discussed earlier, this does not mean that pilots must meet a specific standard or sample size to be valuable. Time, recruitment pools, funding, and ethical considerations often limit data collection. However, although pilots may differ from main studies in process or resources, the decisions and claims they support still rest on inferences that follow the same principles as those of any other study. Problems arise when these principles are set aside simply because a study is called a pilot. Rather than stipulating a special rule for pilot sample sizes, we argue that, as for any study, a pilot's goal determines its inferential demands, and those demands specify what can be extracted from a pilot of a given size.

In general, the more precision one expects from (or attributes to) a pilot-informed decision, the more rigorously the pilot must be designed to deliver it. When a pilot is meant to verify a relatively deterministic property (e.g., whether a randomization procedure works), the demands are minimal, and running a couple of participants as a quick sanity check can provide valuable information. Many pilot questions, however, concern quantities that vary from person to person, such as the average time needed to complete the procedure or the average extent to which a manipulation induces the intended state. Because these quantities vary across individuals, the resulting estimates also vary from sample to sample through sampling error alone. Any pilot-informed decision or claim about such a quantity in future samples (e.g., in the main study) is therefore a statistical inference. While a small pilot is entirely appropriate when what it is meant to deliver is correspondingly modest, problems arise when it is asked to license an inferential claim it was not designed for.

For these more inferential cases, a pilot can still be appropriate, provided it is designed to meet the demands set by its goal. As with a main study, how to meet those demands and when the resulting evidence is "enough" depend on the researcher's inferential framework. Under Bayesian inference, even a small amount of data can update beliefs about the quantities of interest, with the size of the update depending on the strength of the evidence relative to prior uncertainty (Wagenmakers et al., 2018). Under a frequentist framework, the required sample size is set by the inferential goal, whether that involves precision in estimation (e.g., a target confidence-interval width for an ICC) or control of Type I and Type II error rates for a planned decision (Lehmann & Romano, 2005; Neyman & Pearson, 1933). The choice between inferential frameworks, which in turn shapes the necessary sample size, reflects a broader philosophical commitment that extends beyond the scope of piloting (for guidelines, see Gelman & Carlin, 2014; Lakens, 2022).

Taken together, confidence in pilot-informed decisions should be calibrated to whether the pilot's design matches its purpose, regardless of the "pilot" label itself. Because the appropriateness of any pilot depends on what it is being asked to deliver, we advocate treating piloting as methodological due diligence rather than a guarantor of validity.

Transparency as a Condition for Validity

Our call for more piloting rests on the assumption that pilot evidence is used in a principled and transparent manner. We have articulated ways in which piloting can be understood and outlined a breadth of validity-relevant uses. However, no matter how they are used, pilot studies cannot improve validity assessment if they are not reported alongside the final studies they inform. When substantive design or analytic choices are justified by pilot findings, readers and reviewers need sufficient information to evaluate whether those inferences are warranted. This means being explicit about what the pilot was designed to reveal, which data belong to the pilot versus the main study, and what updates or downstream decisions it can reasonably support.

Otherwise, even if one were to adopt a piloting approach of the kind we recommend, the main study could be carefully planned while the evidential basis for its design decisions remains largely invisible, and the broader evaluation and credibility concerns motivating this paper would remain unaddressed. Similarly, as outlined in the introduction, piloting can supply the design information that preregistration calls for but does not itself provide; but without transparent reporting, it can also displace that difficulty rather than resolve it. Pilot-stage decisions propagate into the main study's design and analysis, and the consequences of poor inference at the pilot stage compound into the main. Transparent reporting is therefore a precondition for any validity assessment that piloting is designed to support.

Recent methodological work echoes this concern that the systematic evaluation of validity is central to research quality control, and this can only happen with transparent reporting. Schiavone et al. (2023) argue that "evaluating the validity of the authors' claims is essential to the function of peer review" (p. 6), and Kerschbaumer et al. (2025) developed a checklist intended to support researchers in monitoring validity across the planning, data collection, analysis, and reporting stages of a study. Dreber and Toussaert (2026) extend this to piloting, noting that to establish a rigorous scientific workflow, it is important that pilot studies are used to test logistics. However, following Handley-Miner et al. (2025), they also highlight that pilots need to be disclosed for this process to translate into genuine research quality. Thus, returning to Bem's (2011) question about pilot exploration, we argue that when pilot evidence shapes the design or analysis of the subsequent study, it should form part of that study's evidential record (see also Holzmeister et al., 2024).

Limitations and Open Questions

Our argument for piloting as a tool for strengthening validity has several caveats that are worth acknowledging. First, piloting is one tool among several for addressing validity problems. For some questions, simulations (e.g., Pfaffel et al., 2016), meta-analyses (e.g., Farrar et al., 2020; Roth et al., 2005), or existing large-scale datasets may more efficiently provide the relevant information. Our goal is to encourage the uptake of piloting and its transparent reporting, not to prescribe it as a universal workflow.

Second, the functional definition we adopt is itself a position. There is relatively little systematic evidence on how piloting is practiced across psychological subfields, and survey work suggests that what counts as a pilot varies widely (Pilot Reporting Task Force, 2024). Open questions therefore remain about pilot typology in psychology and what adequate practice looks like across paradigms and subfields.

Third, the promises of piloting we have outlined assume a level of transparency that is not currently the norm in psychology (Handley-Miner et al., 2025). To fully establish piloting's relevance to validity assessment, the field will need to develop the reviewer expectations and dedicated reporting conventions that make "principled and transparent" piloting actionable.

Conclusion

Concerns about validity have spurred many tools for identifying threats, but researchers still need concrete ways to evaluate their planned study early enough to make adjustments. We propose treating piloting as a structured way to learn about one's own study in advance, and as scientific evidence when used to justify design or analytic choices. When conducted with principled aims and reported transparently, piloting can help researchers identify validity threats early, reduce uncertainty in planning, and avoid common pitfalls. Piloting, understood in this way, should play a central role in psychologists' scientific toolkit.

Figure 2. Pitfalls: Ways Piloting Can Harm Validity Note. Entries describe ways piloting can undermine research validity when basic principles of inference are not followed. These pitfalls are not inherent to piloting itself, but arise from specific misuses or misinterpretations of pilot data.

For simplicity, this paper uses the terms "pilot studies", "pilots", and "piloting." However, pilot studies are also commonly referred to as "preliminary studies," "feasibility studies," "pretests," or "pre-tests." In some contexts, preliminary studies may also be described as pre-study manipulation checks or norming studies. We return to possible implications of this terminological variation in the Discussion.

These thresholds should be specified before the pilot data are examined and should be unrelated to the focal hypothesis of the main study.

One might ask where estimating focal effect sizes for a main study's power analysis fits within this framework. We generally treat this as a boundary case rather than a core function of piloting, because either the pilot has the inferential structure that makes it indistinguishable from the main study, or it lacks that structure and likely cannot reliably inform planning(Albers & Lakens, 2018; see also Figure2). This differs from using pilot data to estimate auxiliary design parameters, such as outcome variance, intraclass correlations, missing-data rates, or valid-trial counts, which can inform sample-size planning without estimating the focal effect. However, given the diversity of research practices, there are likely exceptions to this boundary, and we acknowledge that some subfields already have institutionalized practices for publishing such pilots as standalone articles (e.g., clinical subfields). This is why we maintain that transparent reporting of what was actually done in "piloting" is essential to interpreting any use-case against our definition, so that the claims are always open to evaluation (regardless of one's definitional stance).
